newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl coalition fends off business attacks on tax.
newsitem.headline: Kohl coalition fends off business attacks on tax.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition on Monday defended itself against an attack attack by Germany's business lobby on changes to tax reforms which would cost large companies billions of marks next year.

Business leaders at the weekend criticised amendments pushed through by coalition parties in parliament's finance committee which would hit power utilities hardest and also drastically limit tax writeoffs against company losses.

Leading the critics, BDI industry federation head Hans-Olaf Henkel called the changes a "scandal". BASF chairman Juergen Strube said the government had "lost control" and would drive investment and jobs abroad.
But Peter Jacoby, a budget spokesman for Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), replied that the attacks were overdone.
"Talking about a disastrous impact on business....would be getting things the wrong way round," Jacoby told Saarland radio.
Rainer Bruederle, deputy chairman of coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), also accused big business of crying wolf.
He said that while some large firms might come out worse off, Germany's 'Mittelstand' of smaller firms would gain.
"We had to take this path. We expect huge revenue gaps next year. We would not have made it without some costs. It is second best, but the best was not possible," he told InfoRadio.

Industry leaders had lobbied in favour of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's original plan to cut top-rate corporation tax from 45 percent now to 35 percent by 1999, while simplifying the tax system by scrapping a plethora of exemptions.

Their reasoning was that, even though the reforms would not bring significant net tax cuts for business, cutting Germany's high marginal corporate tax rate would encourage investment and help reduce unemployment now above 11 percent.

But power generators have now threatened legal action after hearing that the loss of exemptions on reserves built up to pay to shut down nuclear plants would cost them four billion marks ($2.3 billion) in 1998.
And other big companies said that they would be hit hardest by plans to slash the limit on tax writeoffs allowed against loss-carryovers, costing 1.6 billion marks next year.
Hans Peter Stihl, head of the Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT), on Monday moderated his sharp attack on the tax changes but said it was still wrong to tax company losses.
"You are trampling on the idea of rewarding achievement if the state wants to take its share not just of profits, but of losses too," Stihl said.
Business condemnation was not, however, unanimous. Michael Fuchs, head of the German Federation of Wholesalers and Foreign Trade (BGA) said the attacks were "completely over the top".
He said reductions in writeoff opportunities would be more than offset by tax cuts, and the changes would help investment by making Germany's tax system more transparent.
Newspapers said the centre-right government had scored an own-goal by trying to extract extra cash from its natural allies in business to help reach borrowing targets for Europe's single currency.
"The coalition is doing its best finally to gamble away its last mark: the business view that it is more financially competent than the opposition," the Handelsblatt daily wrote.
Waigel's amended tax bills are expected to pass their second and third readings in the Bundestag lower house of parliament this Thursday.

But they face certain rejection on July 4 in the Bundesrat, which is controlled by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), opening the way for lengthy horse-trading in parliament's mediation process before standing any chance of becoming law.
